title: Appeals Court Rejects Trump's Bid to Keep His Name on the Kennedy Center
summary: President Trump has lost another round in the legal battle over the Kennedy Center's decision to strip his name from the iconic arts complex. On Wednesday, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit unanimously denied his request for an emergency stay. The signage on the building's facade has been hidden under tarp and scaffolding since June 13, and Executive Director Matt Floca confirmed in a court filing last month that Trump's name has already been physically removed. Trump's legal team argued that the removal would cause "irreparable injury"—wasting time and money already spent, and threatening future fundraising. But the judges, Patricia Millett, Robert Wilkins, and Gregory Katsas, were unpersuaded. They wrote that since the name is already off, "a stay would not avert those harms." More pointedly, they said Trump's claims about financial decline were backed only by "conclusory assertions" from Floca in a "factually unsupported declaration." The ruling is the latest in a lawsuit filed by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) against Trump and the Kennedy Center board. The presiding judge, Christopher R. Cooper, has ordered a status report on the center's operations and programming by the end of July. The Kennedy Center's current calendar reflects a dramatically scaled-back lineup. Once home to over 2,000 annual events, including free daily Millennium Stage performances, it now lists only a handful of July offerings: outdoor movie screenings, children's workshops, and five free live shows. The legal fight underscores the ongoing tension over the center's direction and the symbolic weight of Trump's name on a national cultural institution.
why_it_matters: The fight over whose name adorns a major cultural institution reveals how easily the arts can become a political battlefield, where a building's identity can shape public memory. For young people who might perform or visit there, the shrunken calendar is a clear consequence—symbolic battles can have real, tangible effects on community access to the arts.

background_read: The Kennedy Center (a performing arts center in Washington, D.C., named after President John F. Kennedy) opened in 1971 as a living memorial and hosts thousands of events yearly, including the free daily Millennium Stage performances. Its board of trustees includes presidential appointees, which can make naming decisions politically charged.

During his presidency (2017-2021), Trump's name was added to the Kennedy Center after a board vote. After he left office, the board decided to remove it, sparking a legal fight that has now reached the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit (the second-highest federal court, just below the Supreme Court).
Rep. Joyce Beatty (a Democratic congresswoman from Ohio) filed the lawsuit, arguing that the board's decision to strip Trump's name was proper and should be upheld.

perspectives.description: Those who support removing Trump's name believe it restores the center's nonpartisan mission and keeps a national cultural icon free from association with any one politician's legacy. They see the board's move as a necessary correction that protects the arts from being overshadowed by a single personality.

Trump's supporters view the removal as a petty, politically motivated erasure that wastes donor money and could discourage future philanthropy for the arts. They argue that stripping the name harms fundraising and sends a message that cultural institutions are hostile to conservative donors.

Legally, the case tests how far boards can go in undoing naming rights and whether a former official can claim irreparable injury when the name is already gone. The court's dismissal of unsupported financial claims highlights the high bar for emergency relief, but the lawsuit over the board's authority is far from over.

The eventual ruling could set a precedent for how publicly funded venues handle controversial name removals, possibly spurring new legislation on naming rights and donor agreements. If the board prevails, it may embolden other institutions to reconsider names attached during divisive periods; if Trump wins, it could limit future removal efforts.
